newsitem.title: INDIA: Bulls party in India stocks, eye oil price hike.
newsitem.headline: Bulls party in India stocks, eye oil price hike.

text.p: Latecomers could keep the bull rally alive in Indian shares this week after funds drove the Bombay index to a one-year high.
But some analysts cautioned the bulls might have charged too fast and that the market needed to consolidate before moving higher.
"There's so much money flowing into the system, liquidity is easing," Prashant Purker, head of institutional sales at Peregrine Capital India, told Reuters.
"The outlook remains firm and positive next week."
On Friday, Bombay's 30-share blue-chip index cruised to a 12-month high at 4,065 in mid-session. It closed at 4,029.99, surpassing its old high of 4,029.56 set in March this year.
For the week, the Bombay index surged 194 points, or five percent, topping a 3.5 percent rally the previous week.
Analysts said India's cheap valuations were attracting foreign investors while other Asian markets remained dogged by uncertainties.
"There is a problem with most other Asian economies and that also helps Indian stocks," said Ajay Srinivasan, chief investment officer at ITC-Threadneedle Asset Management.
Brokers said the rally was focused on shares of multinational and state-run firms, with penny stocks ignored.
"Every stock is nice and positive," said Maulik Sharedalal, a member-broker of the Bombay Stock Exchange. "The rally is quite broadbased, mid-cap stocks are also moving up."
Some traders said the consistent rise in share prices over the past fortnight lured more buyers, with big local funds also halting supply of shares, thus helping build momentum.
"Good management stocks such as Cadbury and Nestle and front-line stocks are going up," Peregrine's Purker said.
"The market has been undervalued for quite some time and we saw a lot of pent-up demand that came about."
The Bombay index has rocketed 345 points, or about 10 percent, in the past 12 sessions.
Despite the sharp run-up, most analysts said a consolidation could pave the way for further gains.
"I just hope the markets come down a bit. Five percent in one week is a bit too much," said ITC-Threadneedle's Srinivasan.
The impending rise in government-set oil prices that has weighed on the markets could be decided as early as Monday.
But the price rise was probably already discounted because a move by the government had been expected for weeks, traders said.
A meeting of the coalition government's Steering Committee was tentatively scheduled for 5 p.m. (1130 GMT) on Monday to take up the oil price issue.

Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral and Finance Minister P. Chidambaram have been pressing for increases in petroleum product prices, while left-wing parties in the coalition want alternatives to be considered.
A decision has been deferred several times already.
